column3: Exact parallel: denial is enacted by turning away, abandoning both response and accessible nearness.
Pharaoh supplies a tyrannical setting in which a divine summons can be resisted; the link is indirect.
Defines closeness as following a received direction in practice, the positive counterpart to turning away.
Exact parallel: active denial and reversal from guidance may open into a rival claim of authority; counter-narration is also possible.
Places the conduct of 75:32 within the approaching resurrection scene, where ordinary sight is disrupted.
Directly joins denial and turning away as a twofold refusal whose stated consequence is punishment.
Shows turning away as visible withdrawal and selected attention, not merely an inward position.
The immediate preceding pair gives 75:32 its behavioral sequence: neither assent nor prayer, then denial and withdrawal.
Turning from the messenger is followed by incompatible dismissive labels, rejecting both source and reception of the message.
Departure and turning become a double retreat that the summons reverses into unavoidable encounter; it can also include abandoned kinship duties.
The immediate continuation presents withdrawal as returning home with self-satisfied bearing.
The repeated priority wording may suggest an approaching claim upon the person, but the connection is tenuous.
Contrasts denial with an inner faculty that does not falsify what it apprehends; failure of cognition is only a secondary link.
Creation of the heavens and earth supplies a resurrection-capacity frame for the later accounting of 75:32.
Names ongoing deniers as liable to woe, treating denial as a sustained stance before manifest evidence.
Its insistence that they wronged themselves offers a broad consequence frame, with little specific contact with turning away.
Part of the immediate cosmic sequence that makes the refusal in 75:32 answerable before a disrupted world.
The next warning reverses attempted withdrawal: the fitting consequence comes near and has priority over the person.
Divine nearness despite unseen perception counters the illusion that one can withdraw from the final encounter.
Closes the passage with resurrection power, grounding the accountability implied by 75:32.
Protective allegiance is a direction-setting commitment, with a limited danger exception; it only broadly illuminates turning.
The contrastive wording alone adds no focused evidence about denial and turning away.
A commanded responsive relation to the Prophet provides a distant positive contrast to the refusal in 75:32.
Treats allegiance as a chosen direction, but its family-loyalty setting is secondary to 75:32.
Collective denial of messengers supplies a recurring communal pattern for the individual formulation in 75:32.
Continues the immediate resurrection horizon in which the conduct of 75:32 is judged.
Supporters reverse into retreat under pressure; turning back can expose a failed allegiance, though the setting differs.
The contrast between creation in truth and ignorance is too general to sharpen 75:32.
Repetition makes the approaching, warranted consequence persistent across the passage rather than a single warning.
After a covenant, turning away may mean leaving its protective order, but this is an auxiliary extension.
Distinguishes denying the messenger from rejecting God's signs, locating the refusal at the level of signs and injustice.
The ensuing question rejects the idea of being left without purpose, supplying the accountability denied in 75:32.
God's protective nearness and help form a positive relational counterpoint to withdrawal.
Pairs denial with disobedience, showing a cognitive rejection carried into conduct; neglected entrusted response is a secondary nuance.
Another collective messenger-denial pattern reinforces that the wording can mark a recurrent public refusal.
Turning from remembrance is a chosen diversion of attention; reciprocal withdrawal can limit an unproductive closed channel.
Turning away redirects attention from displayed signs, while disbelief covers what was available to be seen.
The grim faces in the immediate resurrection scene visualize the outcome of the preceding refusal.
Presents a turning individual as a case assessed through visible conduct; severed nearness is a secondary reading.
Denial of the best is set against giving and beneficial action, and may also collapse in the claimed self-sufficiency.
Human formation within the same passage turns the warning from bare threat into an argument from created origin.
May expose practical denial through living as though passing gifts endure, but this is indirect.
Generalizes denial of messengers as a repeated pattern whose stated consequence becomes due.
The appeal to ancestral custom may illustrate a defensive frame for denial, without directly naming the act here.
Denial is tested by a crushing outcome; it also recurs beyond past peoples, while a self-defeating accusation remains only a secondary possibility.
Denial of the Hour is answered by a fire already prepared, making rejected future judgment present in the warning.
The immediate fearful expectation of calamity gives the warning after 75:32 an embodied anticipatory face.
Turning from the true account can be read as corruptive departure, but the social consequence is auxiliary.
The refrain casts denial as continued rejection across a cumulative evidentiary record; its failed rival claim is secondary.
Sexual differentiation continues the passage's formation argument behind the accountability of 75:32.
Withdrawal can be reframed as prudent foresight and celebrated, illustrating a self-justifying evasive posture.
The repeated woe moves from historical destruction to evidence in human formation, widening the setting of denial.
Status-based demands may be a form of resistance to a messenger, but the connection remains indirect.
The command to turn from them shifts from avoidable warning to an unavoidable summons, without making both turns equivalent.
Previous messengers were denied despite clear proofs, making denial a recurrent response rather than a defect in delivery.
The immediate denial of refuge removes any imagined escape from the consequence following 75:32.
After signs become visible, the refrain collapses denial before sensory evidence and leads toward silencing; failed counterclaim is secondary.
A fortified community's denial can suggest a closed reception of every messenger; the spatial metaphor is auxiliary.
Repeats the Pharaoh mission setting: resistance to a summons confronts tyrannical excess, indirectly framing 75:32.
Chosen allegiance to God, messenger, and believers is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
Here turning away bears grief in the body rather than rejection, preserving a contrary use of the motion.
The immediate destination to the Lord makes the prior withdrawal unable to alter final return.
Priority can denote being most due for encounter with the Fire, directly illuminating the warning language after 75:32.
Opposed truth-claims await disclosure of who receives disgrace and who is false; its relation is general.
A known appointed term supports an ordered judgment horizon, but does not directly clarify denial or turning.
Repeated instruction to turn away until a time marks restraint after warning, unlike the culpable withdrawal of 75:32.
Pairs fabrication about God with denial of His signs and denies success to such injustice.
The immediate being-driven to the Lord reverses any apparent self-directed departure in 75:32.
Being immersed in denial makes it a continuing enclosing condition; it cannot erase the protected message, though hostile campaign is secondary.
Fabricating about God and denying His signs are opposite distortions of source and truth, neither yielding lasting success.
Introduces the Moses account whose later denial and disobedience offer a narrated parallel.
Explicitly forbids turning away while hearing, making withdrawal a failure of responsive listening and communal obedience.
Fabrication adds unauthorized speech to God while denying truth removes what has arrived; both misplace truth's authority.
The oath by resurrection establishes the governing horizon for the refusal and warning in 75:32.
Withdrawal after unpriced service is a contrary, non-rejecting use that opens receptivity to provision.
Past communities' denial shows a repeating social response while preserving the messenger's completed duty of clear delivery.
Determined formation supports ordered agency and judgment, but only indirectly addresses the conduct in 75:32.
Priority is a structured claim over believers, distinguished from kinship and friendship; it illuminates the warning's relational force.
Turning in allegiance can create functional closeness without true belonging, exposing divided and deceptive affiliation.
The immediate faces looking toward their Lord provide the positive directional counterpart to turning away.
Turning can be purposive orientation without confining God to place, a distant semantic counterpoint to moral withdrawal.
Earlier peoples denied signs even when made manifest, locating refusal after evidence and within warning.
Guidance toward the Lord and reverent fear offer a positive alternative to denial and withdrawal.
Divine guardianship is effective protective nearness for believers, contrasted with the absence of such a guardian for disbelievers.
Denial can precede both adequate knowledge and the arrival of interpretation; prior outcomes reopen this premature judgment.
The radiant faces of the immediate scene form the visible counterstate to the dark faces tied to feared consequence.
Denial initiates a process in which warned punishment tests which claim endures in the world.
Denial follows messengers who brought clear proofs and scripture, excluding mere non-arrival as an explanation.
Showy worship may offer a behavioral foil to genuine prayer, but it only indirectly bears on 75:31-32.
Partial recognition may be a possible contrary reading of denial, yet this connection is too slight for more weight.
Incompatible allegiances can reveal deficient belief, adding a relational form of turning away.
Denying addressed signs accumulates failed response and transgression, with punishment linked to that ongoing conduct.
The immediate recognition of separation gives the final, personal horizon of the withdrawal described in 75:32.
Repeated deeds shape the protective relation in which one lives; divine guardianship is the lived result of a practiced path.
Broad mercy does not cancel punishment for criminal rejection, preserving both delay and irreversible consequence.
When people turn away, reliance is returned to God's sufficiency without claiming control over their response.
The contrastive statement about provision and ignorance does not materially clarify 75:32.
Physical inability is distinguished from willing withdrawal, separating excuse from culpable turning and retaining the punishment contrast.
Diverse guidance and misguidance culminate in questioning about deeds, a broad agency-and-accountability frame.
Turning away does not halt the task: another people can replace the refusers without repeating their pattern.
Explicitly binds obedience to God and the messenger with the alternative of turning away, then names the refusers as disbelievers.
Turning away is contrasted with obeying the messenger; the messenger is not made a controller over the refuser.
Commands obedience and warns that turning away leaves the messenger's duty as clear delivery, separating proclamation from response.
Denial of God's signs together with averting from them closely combines rejection and active disengagement.
Those who deny the signs and act arrogantly toward them provide a conduct-based parallel to denial followed by withdrawal.
After rejecting and seeking to harm, turning away is met with punishment in this world and the next.
A revealed surah is met with mutual glances and departure, portraying withdrawal from disclosed guidance as a social act.
The call to return and obey is followed by fear of a great-day punishment if they turn away, closely matching 75:32's horizon.
If they turn away after the message has been conveyed, the consequence is placed beyond the messenger's control.
Turning away leaves only the completed duty of clear communication, a direct counterpart to responsive acceptance.
Turning from remembrance has an enduring consequence, extending 75:32's withdrawal beyond the immediate scene.
A declared warning remains in force when they turn away; the exact time of what is promised is not claimed by the warner.
Turning one's side to mislead gives bodily posture a morally directed, oppositional force.
A profession of belief and obedience is exposed when a group then turns away, separating claim from enacted response.
Avoiding God's and the messenger's judgment is described as turning away, a concrete institutional form of withdrawal.
When signs are recited, arrogant turning as though unheard gives a vivid model of deliberate non-reception.
Being reminded of God's signs and then turning away is explicitly marked as grave wrongdoing.
Turning away after clarification is answered with warning of a destructive consequence, preserving the warning-response structure.
If they turn away, the messenger remains a conveyor rather than a keeper over them, a parallel to refusal without coercion.
Retreat after guidance becomes clear portrays reversal from received direction and its enabling deceptive promise.
Turning heads away from a call to forgiveness makes withdrawal visible as proud bodily refusal.
Obedience is commanded; if they turn away, the messenger's obligation remains clear delivery.
Turning from the reminder depicts flight from admonition, a strong image of evasion that complements 75:32.
Hearing recitation without prostration supplies a close behavioral counterpart to the absence of prayer before 75:32.
The following denial shows that failure to respond to recitation and active rejection can operate as one sequence.
